summary: Defines a remote procedure call that compares two management datastores on a network device and reports the differences. It works with datastores described by the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA), for example the running configuration and the one actually in use. The operation helps operators see how configuration differs between states.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a spot-the-difference game for two copies of a device's settings, showing exactly what changed.

questions: what is the nmda compare rpc
how to compare intended and operational datastores
subtitle: A NETCONF and RESTCONF operation that asks a device to diff two of its datastores, such as intended versus operational.

tldr.problem: With NMDA, the same data can sit in several datastores, and what a user intended can differ from what is really in effect. Fetching both datastores and comparing them is costly and wasteful.
tldr.mechanism: A new YANG RPC, compare, takes a source and target datastore plus optional filter, all and report-origin parameters. The server returns the differences as a YANG Patch.
tldr.outcome: Operators can see where applied configuration departs from intended configuration without moving whole datastores. The operation can be expensive, so access control and rate limiting are advised.

today: RFC 9144 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the ietf-nmda-compare module.

sections.title: Why Compare Datastores
sections.content:
The Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342) introduces datastores that each give a different viewpoint on YANG-defined data. <intended> holds validated configuration a client wants in effect. <operational> holds operational state, such as statistics, plus configuration that is actually in effect.

Data moves from one datastore to another, so differences can appear. Some are expected, because there can be a time lag between configuration reaching <intended> and taking effect. Others come from unmet conditions, inactive parts of the configuration, unresolved resource dependencies or implementation errors. They can hide the true status of the network, harm services and misallocate resources.

A client could fetch both datastores and compare them itself, but the RFC calls that costly and extremely wasteful. RFC 9144 instead lets the server do it, with RPCs used over NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040).
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine writing a to-do list and a helper writing what they actually did. This lets you ask for just the differences instead of reading both lists.

sections.title: The compare Operation
sections.content:
The core is one new RPC, <compare>. It checks for differences in values or in data nodes present in either datastore. The input parameters are:

  • source: the reference datastore, for example <intended>.
  • target: the datastore compared against it, for example <operational>.
  • filter-spec: a subtree filter or an XPath filter that limits the comparison to part of the datastore. It cannot match on data node values.
  • all: include all differences, including schema nodes present in only one datastore. Without it, the server first drops schema nodes not present in both.
  • report-origin: include origin metadata. It is omitted by default and applies only when <operational> is involved.

The prefiltering when all is absent lets clients focus on real mismatches of instance data without writing more complex filters.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the device which two lists to compare, and optionally which part of them. By default it ignores items that could only ever exist in one list.

sections.title: Output and the YANG Module
sections.content:
The output is either no-matches, meaning the filter matched nothing so nothing was compared, or differences. Differences use the YANG Patch format of RFC 8072, so the result is the patch that would turn the source into the target. The data model augments each edit with a source-value so the reader also sees the source's value.

A node in the source that is missing from the target may be reported as either delete or remove, since the comparison does not distinguish them. When the target is <operational> and report-origin is set, origin metadata is included. This can explain a difference, for example when a node in <intended> has origin system in <operational>.

The module is named ietf-nmda-compare, with prefix cmp, and its tree notation follows RFC 8340.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a list of edits, like tracked changes in a document, that would make the first list match the second.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC compares an interface in <operational> (the source) with <intended> (the target). In <intended>, interface eth0 has enabled set to false and a description. In <operational> it is true with no description, and its origin is learned.

The reply holds two edits. Edit 1 is a replace of enabled with the target value false, plus a source-value of true with its origin. Edit 2 is a create of description with the value ip interface. The RFC shows the exchange in NETCONF XML and in RESTCONF JSON.
sections.plainLanguage: One list says the lamp is off and has a label. The other says the lamp is on and has no label. The answer says: turn it off and add the label.

sections.title: Performance Costs
sections.content:
The operation can be computationally expensive. Clients are expected to use it sparingly, and implementations must make sure that heavy use does not hurt system performance. One suggested mitigation is to limit how many requests are served to a client, or to all clients, in a time interval, rejecting requests that come too often.

Models for monitoring server resources and RPC rates are outside the scope of this document. Any such model should be general and not limited to this RPC.
sections.plainLanguage: Comparing big lists takes effort. If too many people ask at once, the device should say no to some so it does not get tired out.

sections.title: Access Control and Abuse
sections.content:
The module is accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF. Their mandatory-to-implement secure transports are SSH (RFC 6242) for NETCONF and TLS (RFC 8446) for RESTCONF. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content. NACM rules are per server, so they apply equally to all datastores, and subtrees the requestor cannot read are silently skipped in the comparison.

The <compare> RPC may be sensitive. An attacker could flood a server with comparison requests. Servers can guard against this by requiring authorization through NACM and by limiting the number of requests served to a client in a time interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Only people with permission should be allowed to ask, and anything they are not allowed to see is left out of the answer.

sections.title: Possible Future Extensions
sections.content:
Appendix A sketches one extension, dampening. A client would give a minimum period for which a difference must persist before it is reported. That separates fleeting differences from ones that may show a real inconsistency inside the device.

An extra input parameter would carry the dampening period. A value of 0, or omitting it, means no dampening, and reports MAY be delayed by the period. A server could run a comparison when the RPC arrives, store the result, and after the period check which differences remain.
sections.plainLanguage: Dampening means waiting a moment before reporting a difference, to be sure it is not just a blink that goes away on its own.

data.title: Compare request (JSON)
data.code:
POST /restconf/operations/ietf-nmda-compare:compare HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/yang-data+json
Accept: application/yang-data+json

{ "ietf-nmda-compare:input" : {
   "source" : "ietf-datastores:operational",
   "target" : "ietf-datastores:intended",
   "report-origin" : null,
   "xpath-filter" : "/ietf-interfaces:interfaces"
   }
}
